first.rationale: Onboarding completion and activation are both declining, and prior evidence indicates that reducing onboarding friction improves completion, time-to-value, and early adoption. Promotional pricing directly addresses competitive pressure but previously caused materially worse 30-day retention, conflicting with the sustainable qualified-revenue objective. Verify the onboarding result and the pricing retention tradeoff before committing the single experiment slot.

mid.rationale: Run a standard experiment simplifying onboarding. The verified prior produced +13% completion, 2.1-day faster time-to-value, and +3% 30-day retention, directly addressing both current declines while supporting sustainable revenue. Promotional pricing is rejected despite competitor pressure because its +18% qualified-revenue lift came with a verified 12% retention decline and failure by first renewal. Maintain an experimental holdout because the prior onboarding result may not transfer perfectly to current users.

final2.rationale: Proceed with onboarding simplification. Verified evidence shows +13% completion, 2.1-day faster time-to-value, and +3% 30-day retention, directly supporting sustainable qualified revenue while addressing current onboarding and activation declines. The competitor’s deeper cut and increased churn conversations raise urgency but do not overturn verified evidence that a 40% SMB discount reduced 30-day retention by 12% and failed through first renewal. The pricing signal may warrant a separately designed retention response next cycle, but broad promotional pricing is not justified now.
